5.title: Beyond the Lesson
5.passage:
When people decide to learn a language, they often begin by looking for the right course, teacher or app. That makes sense: organised lessons provide structure, clear goals and someone to explain what is going on. Yet many learners discover that progress does not depend only on what happens during those scheduled hours. The real change often begins later, when the lesson has ended and the language starts appearing in ordinary life. At that point, learning can feel less like completing tasks and more like joining a conversation that has been continuing without you.

For years, language experts have encouraged students to practise outside the classroom, but this advice is easy to misunderstand. Some learners imagine they must move abroad, find native-speaker friends immediately or spend every evening studying grammar. In fact, out-of-class learning is usually far less dramatic. It may involve following a chef on social media, listening to football podcasts on the way to work, changing a phone setting or reading comments under videos. These activities might appear too small to matter, especially when they are done irregularly. However, their value lies partly in the fact that they connect the language with habits that already exist.

This matters because classroom learning and everyday contact with a language do different jobs. In class, students are often protected from confusion. A text is chosen because it contains useful vocabulary; a listening task is designed so that key information can be identified; errors are corrected before they become permanent. Outside the classroom, by contrast, language arrives in a messier form. People speak too fast, joke without explanation and refer to things the learner has never heard of. That experience can be frustrating, but it also trains an important skill: learning to continue even when full understanding is impossible. Successful learners are not always the ones who understand everything. Often, they are the ones who stop panicking when they do not.

There is, however, a risk in praising independent learning too much. It can sound as if teachers no longer matter, or as if students who cannot travel or meet speakers face an impossible task. Neither is true. Teachers remain important because they help learners notice patterns they would otherwise miss, and because they save time by directing attention towards what is worth learning next. At the same time, modern learners have access to opportunities that previous generations could barely imagine. They may never leave home and still hear different accents, join online gaming groups or watch live interviews from another continent. Access does not guarantee improvement, of course, but it has changed what is possible.

Another mistake is to assume that enjoyable exposure automatically leads to progress. Watching ten crime series in another language may improve listening confidence, but only if the learner is engaged in some active way. That does not mean turning every film into homework. It may be enough to replay a short section, copy an expression that keeps appearing or notice how speakers disagree politely. Small acts of attention turn entertainment into material for learning. Without that attention, learners can remain comfortable for months while understanding little more than they did at the start.

Perhaps the biggest advantage of learning beyond the classroom is psychological. Lessons are useful, but they can accidentally suggest that a language belongs inside textbooks and exercises. Meeting it elsewhere changes that impression. A learner who orders a meal, laughs at a joke online or understands part of a song receives a different message: this language is not simply a subject to be passed, but a tool for doing real things. That feeling rarely arrives all at once. More often, it grows through dozens of small encounters which seem unimportant on their own. Together, they can produce the moment every learner wants: the point at which the language begins to feel less foreign, and more like part of daily life.

questions.prompt: What point does the writer make in the opening paragraph about learning a language?
options: A) Formal lessons are mainly useful for people who need clear explanations.
B) Real progress often begins when learners start meeting the language in everyday situations.
C) Most learners lose motivation once the organised part of a course has finished.
D) People usually choose language courses before deciding what they want to use the language for.
questions.evidence: The writer says progress does not depend only on lessons and that 'the real change often begins later' when the language 'starts appearing in ordinary life'.
questions.rationale: B is correct because it captures the central idea of the paragraph: learning develops more deeply when the language becomes part of daily experience. A is too narrow: the paragraph says lessons provide structure and explanations, but that is not the main point. C is unsupported; the writer does not mention learners losing motivation. D is mentioned only indirectly through choosing courses and is not the writer's main message.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer include examples such as following a chef online or changing a phone setting?
options: A) To show that useful language practice can be built into ordinary routines
B) To show that learners need to make major changes to their daily lives to improve
C) To explain why out-of-class activities are more valuable when they are done regularly
D) To suggest that informal activities can replace organised language lessons
questions.evidence: The writer explains that out-of-class learning is 'usually far less dramatic' and that these activities matter because they connect the language with 'habits that already exist'.
questions.rationale: A is correct because the examples illustrate how small, everyday actions can become language practice. B is wrong because the writer says out-of-class learning is 'usually far less dramatic' and needs no upheaval. C inverts the point: the writer concedes these activities are often done irregularly and still count. D is contradicted by the following paragraph, which insists teachers remain important.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what is one benefit of encountering language outside the classroom?
options: A) It allows learners to avoid making errors that later become habits.
B) It gives learners experience of understanding every kind of speaker.
C) It develops the ability to keep going despite uncertainty.
D) It helps learners focus on key facts in a more efficient way.
questions.evidence: The writer contrasts the classroom with messier real-life input and says this 'trains an important skill: learning to continue even when full understanding is impossible'.
questions.rationale: C is correct because the paragraph emphasises resilience and tolerance of partial understanding. A describes what the classroom can do, not out-of-class contact. B is too absolute; the writer says outside language can be difficult and confusing, not that learners end up understanding every kind of speaker. D again refers to classroom tasks designed to identify key information.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude towards independent learning in the fourth paragraph?
options: A) doubtful that it can work for learners without strong teacher support
B) worried that it has become less useful because of technology
C) enthusiastic because it has replaced older teaching methods
D) positive about its possibilities, while warning against unrealistic claims
questions.evidence: The writer says there is 'a risk in praising independent learning too much' and rejects the idea that teachers no longer matter, while also noting that modern learners have many new opportunities.
questions.rationale: D is correct because the writer supports independent learning but balances that with cautions about exaggerating it. A is too negative; the writer does not doubt that independent learning can work. B is the opposite of the paragraph, which says technology has expanded opportunities. C is wrong because the writer never suggests independent learning has replaced teachers or classroom methods.

questions.prompt: In the fifth paragraph, what does the writer say about enjoyable exposure to a language?
options: A) It is most helpful when learners treat entertainment as formal study.
B) It can increase confidence, but only leads to progress if learners notice things actively.
C) It works best when learners choose challenging material rather than familiar genres.
D) It is mainly valuable for improving listening, rather than other skills.
questions.evidence: The writer says watching series 'may improve listening confidence, but only if the learner is engaged in some active way' and gives examples of replaying sections or noticing expressions.
questions.rationale: B is correct because it reflects both parts of the writer's point: confidence may grow, but progress requires active attention. A is incorrect because the writer specifically says this does not mean turning every film into homework. C is not stated; there is no contrast between challenging and familiar material. D is too limited because the paragraph is about progress more generally, not only listening.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main purpose in the article as a whole?
options: A) to persuade teachers to give learners fewer controlled classroom tasks
B) to argue that modern technology has solved most difficulties in language learning
C) to explain how learning beyond lessons can support progress when approached realistically
D) to challenge the view that confidence matters more than grammatical accuracy
questions.evidence: Across the article, the writer argues that lessons matter but everyday contact with the language also matters, provided learners use it realistically and with attention.
questions.rationale: C is correct because it summarises the article's balanced message: out-of-class learning is valuable, but not magical, and works best when understood properly. A is too focused on teachers and reducing classroom tasks, which is not the writer's goal. B exaggerates the role of technology and ignores the cautions. D introduces a debate the article does not mainly address.

6.directions: Six sentences have been removed from the article. Choose from the sentences A–G the one which fits each gap. There is one extra sentence which you do not need to use.
6.title: Small Ideas, Big Changes
6.passage:
When people talk about life-changing inventions, they often mention planes, computers or the internet. Yet many of the objects that shape our days are far less dramatic. We use them so automatically that it is easy to forget they had to be designed, tested and accepted by the public. Their importance lies not in how exciting they seem, but in how completely they have blended into ordinary routines. (37) Once that happens, daily life begins to feel different in ways that are hard to reverse.

One good example is the humble zip. Before it became common, buttons, hooks and laces did the same jobs, but usually more slowly and with greater effort. Early versions of the zip were not especially reliable, and some clothing companies worried that customers would not trust them. (38) As manufacturers improved the design, however, people started to appreciate the speed and convenience it offered, especially on children's clothes, bags and boots.

Another invention that transformed everyday life was the ballpoint pen. Cheap, light and easy to carry, it solved a problem that had frustrated writers for years: fountain pens leaked, needed careful refilling and often stopped working at inconvenient moments. The new pen was not instantly perfect, and some early models were disappointing. (39) By the time production methods improved, though, the ballpoint had become practical enough for offices, schools and homes.

The electric washing machine had an even deeper effect because it changed not just a single task but the rhythm of domestic life. Washing clothes by hand was tiring, time-consuming work, and in many homes it occupied a full day every week. (40) This mattered especially in larger families, where the amount of washing could be overwhelming. What had once required constant physical effort gradually became a more manageable background task.

Not every useful invention is mechanical. Supermarkets, for instance, depended on a social invention as much as a technical one: the barcode. Shops had always needed a way to identify products and calculate prices, but doing this by hand was slow and often inaccurate. (41) It also made stock control easier, helping shops know what needed replacing before shelves became empty.

Perhaps the most powerful inventions are the ones that remove tiny obstacles again and again. The sticky note is a good case in point. It was created from an adhesive that was weaker than expected, which might normally have been seen as a failure. Instead, someone realised that a note which could be attached and removed without damage would be useful in offices, classrooms and kitchens. (42) Because they are so simple, we rarely notice how often they save us time.

Inventions like these rarely appear in history books beside grand scientific breakthroughs. Even so, they deserve attention because they show that progress is not always about doing spectacular new things. Sometimes it is about making familiar tasks easier, quicker and slightly less annoying. That quieter kind of innovation may be less impressive at first sight, but it is often what changes everyday life most completely.
sentencePool: A) Once scanners could read it quickly, paying for shopping became faster for customers and less stressful for staff.
B) In fact, many successful inventions become almost invisible precisely because they work so well.
C) For that reason, the first users were not always convinced that it was better than older alternatives.
D) As a result, people could spend more of their time on other responsibilities or on activities they actually enjoyed.
E) Their value comes from being available exactly when a reminder, label or quick message is needed.
F) In some cases, inventors deliberately kept the original materials unchanged in order to protect traditional manufacturing methods.
G) This hesitation meant that the device first appeared on items where practicality mattered more than style.

7.directions: Read the article in which people talk about their experiences. For each question, choose from the people (A–D). The people may be chosen more than once.
7.matchingIntro: Which person…? The people may be chosen more than once.

sections.name: Sophie
sections.text: When my city council proposed to transform an old industrial site into a community garden, I was excited. Initially, I was sceptical about the project's feasibility, given the site's historical contamination. However, after thorough soil treatments and planning, we successfully created a vibrant space. It took teamwork and dedication, but seeing local residents coming together to enjoy the green urban oasis is rewarding. The positive effects on our mental health and community spirit are undeniable. Since then, I've been advocating for additional green projects to enhance urban living. Although some challenges remain, the benefits of having green spaces close to home make it worthwhile. We've also noticed how the garden has made the area feel cleaner and more pleasant. Despite some opposition, particularly from motorists who lost parking spaces, overall, the initiative has been embraced warmly.

sections.name: Liam
sections.text: A few years ago, I initiated a rooftop garden project on top of the commercial building where I work. The primary goal was to reduce the building's energy use and carbon footprint by improving insulation. Initially, raising awareness and funding were challenging, but persistence paid off. The garden now boasts a range of plants that not only beautify the space but also benefit the environment. Colleagues have embraced the opportunity to unwind in the tranquil setting during breaks. Furthermore, it's sparked a noticeable shift in attitudes towards environmental responsibility among staff. There's now a growing interest in expanding similar projects throughout the city. Despite lacking expertise initially, I've learned a lot about sustainable practices. The transformation has been remarkable, and I'm proud to have led this initiative, proving that even small changes can lead to significant impacts.

sections.name: Emily
sections.text: As a city planner, I've always prioritised integrating nature within urban developments. My latest project faced numerous obstacles, including budget constraints and scepticism from the public. However, the urban park's grand opening marked a turning point. The park, equipped with walking trails and picnic areas, aims to provide residents with a retreat from the bustling city life. Seeing families enjoying the new facilities validated the relentless effort my team invested. Community feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, highlighting the park's role in enhancing quality of life. However, there are ongoing discussions about maintaining the park sustainably. Addressing these challenges is critical, as I believe urban green spaces are essential for future developments. The park's success has encouraged further investment in green initiatives, showing people the tangible benefits of environmental stewardship.

sections.name: Oliver
sections.text: My experience with green urban projects began when I joined a volunteering initiative to revitalise neglected neighbourhood parks. It quickly became evident that many people desire spaces that foster community interaction and add beauty to urban life. At first, coordinating volunteers was tough, but witnessing the transformation of these neglected areas made it worthwhile. There's a unique joy in seeing children play and families gather in spaces they once avoided. Over time, my enthusiasm for green spaces only grew. These projects have taught me the significance of integrating nature into urban settings to combat stress and promote well-being. Although I'd like to see more government funding, community-driven efforts have shown potential to bring about change. The sense of ownership that residents feel towards these spaces contributes significantly to their upkeep and preservation.
